title: Days 80 to 83: Four More Days in Athens
content:
If someone asks me what’s the best part of Athens, the answer for me would be the people I met over the last ten days.

First there was Rodrigo, who bought my bicycle. I spent the most time with him hanging out at the hostel because the weather has been so hot during the day. He’s friends with a bunch of female travelers, Alba, Rosio, and Jenna. Together, we celebrated Rodrigo’s 38th birthday. I bought him a cake because I had told him that if I sell my bicycle before his birthday I would buy him a cake. It turned out that I sold my bike to him. Lol!

I sold my camping gears to an American girl named Sarah. She was also interested in my bike, but Rodrigo was at the hostel before her. I felt bad that I didn’t sell my bike to her and offered to treat her to lunch, but our schedule didn’t align. I hope she bought a bicycle somewhere else.

I also met up with Dale at a cafe. We had met last year in Nicosia, Cyprus. It was great catching up with her in Athens. She’s been traveling for five years and I need to learn from her on how to travel slowly.

At the Athens Hawks hostel, I had to switch to a different room. There I met Daniel, a young Brazilian guy who will try to get a job in Germany. I also met Max, a student studying business law. The three of us grabbed dinner at a gyro restaurant where the waiter didn’t think Max could finish his meal due to its large portion. After Max proved him wrong, the waiter, whose name is Dimitry, gave him a free can of Pepsi. I thought the whole thing was so funny because Max owed me a can of soda after losing a bet on the time of sunset over the mountains.

At night on the hostel rooftop bar, we caught up with our other roommates, Kacey and Catia. They are 18 and 19 years old Australian girls. I learned that Kacey’s mother is an opera singer who might have performed on the stage when my parents were living in New York City in the 90s. In fact, there was a good chance that my parents saw Kacey’s mom perform Madam Butterfly. What a small world!

I played three games of pool with two other roommates, Raf and Zoey. Raf is looking at perspective graduate schools and Zoey is almost done finishing a data science master degree from Columbia University.

Yesterday, after staying at Athens Hawks hostel for nine nights, I finally checked out and met up with Paweł, my Couchers host, near Nea Ionia district. Paweł is such an interesting person. He completed his data science master degree not too long ago and is really interested in data privacy. He’s the first person I met who has GrapheneOS installed on his phone. He showed me a bunch of resources online so I can learn more about privacy tools. Inspired by him, I made changes to my website where I removed Disqus commenting system since they were placing ads on my posts, and deleted Google Analytics in the html header so Google can’t track visitors to my website. Even though I won’t be able to see visitor information, I feel it’s a minor inconvenience for me.

Today, I met Marena and Eduardo. They are a couple who arrived at Paweł’s place and will also be staying with him for two nights. Marena is a singer and Eduardo is a saxophone player. They plan on busking at the Acropolis this afternoon to earn some money before going camping at one of the islands nearby.

I’ve thoroughly enjoyed my time in Athens even though I didn’t go to any islands near Athens. Max and I did spent a morning hiking up to Lycabettus Hill to get a good view of the city and visiting Athens National Garden.

Athens, as a city, reminded me a lot of Philadelphia. It’s gritty in certain areas, such as the neighborhood where the hostel is located. Yet other parts of the city are cleaner and geared toward tourists. I hope to be back in Athens again so I can use it as a base to explore the Greek islands. I just didn’t feel like doing any more exploring now that my bike tour has ended.

Overall, my backpacking trip to Italy and Malta has been great and my bike tour from Wrocław, Poland, to Athens, Greece, has been amazing despite the heat. Tomorrow, I will take the 1 PM flight from Athens to Philadelphia. There are so many things I want to do at home, and I will write up a trip summary when I get back.

title: Days 74 to 79: Five Days in Athens
content:
Over the past five days, I only explored Athens for two of the days. I was too worried about selling my bicycle since that’s what I decided to do.

I listed my bike on Buycycle.com and Facebook Marketplace. There was a buyer from each platform, but I ended up selling my bike, along with the panniers, repair tools and parts, some bike clothing, etc, to Rodrigo, the traveler I had met during the first day of my stay at the hostel. He decided to start his first bicycle tour and ride around Europe and maybe go to Türkiye. It’s his 38th birthday today and he sees a new adventure coming.

I was glad to have sold my bike, but I felt bad because there was a girl from Florida who had contacted on Facebook Marketplace and wanted to buy the bike, too. She was disappointed after I sold it to Rodrigo. But she might buy my camping gears and I will try to help her find another bicycle to purchase in Athens.

As for the city of Athens, I walked to Areopagus Hill to get a good view of the Acropolis, then paid €30 as the entrance fee to go inside the grounds of the Acropolis. I also saw the Parthenon and some ancient temples there.

Yesterday after selling my bike, I took a walking tour with Rodrigo and his friends, Bradley and Lucre, to Philopappos Hill to get another good view of the city. We also went to Anafiotika, a neighborhood in Athens that’s full of buildings painted white. There was also a great view from there.

For lunch, we ended up at a vegan restaurant called Mama Tierra Acropolis. The food was excellent. No wonder it has a 4.9 rating with over 1000 reviews.

At the Athens Hawks hostel, I extended my stay until the 24th. After that I will stay with a Couchers host named Paweł for two nights before getting on my flight to Philadelphia.

I’m glad I sold the bike so I don’t have to find a bike box anymore and flying will be so much easier without a bike.

Total distance from King of Prussia to Athens on my bike: 5485 miles

title: My Priority Apollo
content:
Background

I purchased this bicycle from Priority Bicycles in September 2022 for a retail value of $1999, but it was $2225 in total, including shipping to a local bike shop, have it assembled professionally, and paid sales tax.

2022 Priority Apollo webpage

I used this bicycle for two bike tours. One is from King of Prussia, PA, to Gainesville, FL, in 2023 (1968 miles). The other is from King of Prussia, PA, to Athens, Greece, in 2025-26 (5485 miles). The total odometer mileage is about 7500 miles, or ~12000 km.

I gave this bike the name: Serendipity.

Maintenance

This bicycle has been great and lives up to the low maintenance reputation that Priority advertises. Once I installed Schwalbe Marathon Almotion tubeless tires, I had no flats during my Europe bike tour.

The bike is very quiet when ridden, the gears can be changed when the bike is stopped, and the ride is very smooth. Moreover, during rainy days, the bike doesn’t need its chain to be lubed because it doesn’t have a chain, but a belt. You basically get a free bike wash when it rains.

Here’s some more detailed information about the various components and maintenance videos:

Component Maintenance/Info
Shimano Alfine SG-S7001-11 hub - Oil should be changed every 5000 km
- Use only Shimano SG-S700 oil
- Video: How to change the oil
- PDF: Alfine 11 Hub service manual (oil change instruction starts on page 23)
Gates carbon belt 118 CDX - Can last 30000 km
- Video: How to safely coil a belt
- Video: Belt tension adjustment
- Video: Changing the belt
- Video: Apollo gear adjustment
Bottom bracket 68mm GXP
Spokes - Front wheel: 294mm/ 14G
- Rear wheel: 270mm/ 14G
Rim tape size 28 mm X 11 m WTB TCS
Schwalbe Marathon Almotion (Tubeless) tires - Size: 40-622; 28x1.50; 700x38C
- Pressure: 3.5-5.5 bar (50-70 psi)
- Last between 6000 and 10000 km
- Video: Seal a punctured tire
- Video: Rear flat tire repair
- Video: Remove and install a tire and tube
- Video: Patch an inner tube
Widest tire width 45 mm
Narrowest tire width 28 mm

Conclusion

I hope the next owner can take good care of this bicycle. I enjoyed riding this bike a lot. It’s been a great bike!

Contact

For any questions regarding this bike, you can contact me via the About page. You can also email Priority Bicycles directly. Their customer service is top notch!

title: Days 72 and 73: Ferry from Corfu to Igoumenitsa, then Bus to Athens
content:
Two days ago, I took the 9 AM ferry from Corfu to Igoumenitsa. The ferry ride was about 1:30 hours and it was very scenic with the mountains on both sides.

I stayed at Hotel Astoria in Igoumenitsa, which is very close to the ferry terminal. I didn’t do much in town except for getting some meals. Igoumenitsa seems to be just a place for the ferry with nothing special about it.

The next morning, I went to the bus station and spent €68.20 for a bus ticket to Athens. The price included a €15 fee for the bicycle.

The bus ride was from 8:30 AM to about 4 PM. It was a long ride, but I enjoyed the beautiful mountain scenery while listened to some music.

Once I reached the bus station in Athens, I rode about two miles to Athens Hawks hostel. I was glad that I could store my bicycle in the basement of the hostel.

This hostel is a nice hostel. The rooms are clean and there’s a social area. I met another traveler named Rodrigo in the afternoon. He’s from Uruguay. We went to a Pakistani restaurant near the hostel for dinner then walked around the neighborhood for a little while. It seems I’m in a neighborhood full of immigrants.

I only booked for two nights at the hostel, most likely I will extend a few more nights at least. I need to acquire a cardboard bicycle box, but right now there’s a holiday in Greece. From the WhatsApp Europe Cycling group, I read that most bike shops in Athens are closed due to the holiday. I will have to wait a few days then contact the shops. Meanwhile, I plan to do laundry one last time and explore Athens.

title: Day 71: Ferry from Sarandë to Corfu, Greece
content:
This morning, I spent the last of my Leks on some breakfast items at the local grocery store. As always, I wanted to leave a country without any local currency.

At 9 AM, I rode my bike from Mega Hostel to the Sarandë ferry terminal nearby. I had to park my bike, go through passport control, then come back to the other side of the fence to get my bike and wait with the cars. It was a weird process.

The ferry ride from Sarandë to Corfu, Greece, was only about 1:15 hours. There’s a +1 hour time change in Greece so I arrived at 12:15 PM.

At the port in Corfu, I had to take my bike through passport control, which was very awkward since there were so many people waiting in line. Anyway, I was glad I got through that.

I checked into Casa Mia Studio apartment with the help of the owner, Constantinos. He recommended Ninos, a popular restaurant that serves the local cuisine. After relaxing for a bit, I walked to the ferry terminal ticket office to confirm the cost to take my bicycle onto the ferry is free. Since I had bought the Corfu to Igoumenitsa ferry ticket online I wasn’t sure if there’s a fee for bicycles. As it turns out, there isn’t a fee. Good news for me!

For the rest of the afternoon, I walked to the old town in the town of Corfu. By the way, Corfu is also the name of this Greek island.

I saw the New Venetian Fortress. It seemed like a ruin so I wasn’t impressed. I did have a late lunch at Ninos. I had a traditional veal dish called pastitsada. It was really good.

I walked by Spianada Square before paying €10 for the entrance fee to the Old Fortress of Corfu. That was the highlight of my afternoon. I spent quite some time walking inside. At the top of the fortress, I could see the town of Corfu. I also explored the rest of the fortress, including Saint George’s Church.

When I exited the Old Fortress, I walked on the north shore of Corfu to get back to the apartment. I don’t really know what to do in the apartment. I might go for a late dinner if I get hungry. Tomorrow, I’ll take the 9 AM ferry to Igoumenitsa and be on mainland Greece.

title: Days 68 to 70: Three Days in Sarandë
content:
I didn’t explore much in Sarandë, not even taking a boat ride to do some sightseeing. I just didn’t have the motivation and I didn’t want to withdraw any more money from the ATM since I want to leave Albania without any Leks.

I spent the majority of my time in the hostel coding and vibe coding my redesigned website that you are viewing now. This website is built with Jekyll, the same framework that I used for my photography portfolio website. I added my coding portfolio and a blogging feature, along with the option to add comments easily. Now this website contains all the things I’m interested in, like a portfolio. It’s a one stop shop! Lol.

Also I think this website is much simpler, better looking, faster to load, and no database. All the blog posts have been converted to markdown files from the Blogger atom XML file. This process took me the longest since I had to vibe code some Python scripts to do the transformation. In any case, I’m very happy with the result after working on it for one and half days.

This morning, I took a stroll around the neighborhood and discovered a small beach that the locals go to. I liked the cozy atmosphere and took some photographs as the sun rose above the eastern mountain.

In the dorm room this afternoon I met a new guest named Bajram. I had bought some pasta, sausages, and marinara sauce yesterday so I will cook dinner for both of us since there is enough for two people.

Tomorrow morning, I will take the 10 AM ferry from Sarandë to Corfu, Greece. There are only a few hostels on the island and the one that’s available is about 10 miles away from the ferry port. I decided to book an apartment for a whopping $175 near the port and the old town for one night. The following day, I’ll take another ferry to Igoumenitsa on mainland Greece.

title: Days 66 and 67: Bus from Vlorë to Himarë, then Bike to Sarandë
content:
My last night in Vlorë was terrible. There was one guest, an older fat lady, who complained that she felt cold when the AC was on. It was 30C, or 86F, inside the dorm. I don’t understand how she could be feeling cold when it’s so hot. Of course, Nana sided with her since she has an excuse to not turn on the AC in the room. I slept through the heat and I was not happy.

The next morning, I rode my bike to the bus station hoping to get on the bus to Himarë. When I got there, the driver first wanted 4000 Lek, which is €40, for me and my bicycle. I was told by a fellow the day before that it was only going to be 700 Lek, so needless to say I was shocked by the price. Then the driver reduced the price to 3000 Lek, saying 1000 Lek for me and 2000 Lek for my bicycle. I knew I was getting scammed.

I asked other drivers regarding the fare, they all told me 3000 Lek to Himarë. I realized it’s now too late to start cycling to Himarë and there’s a massive hill that I have to cycle over, not to mention the distance. I decided to get scammed so I didn’t have to cycle.

This was the first time that I got scammed in Albania. I guess not all Albanians are good people. Actually, not all people are good people. There will be some bad apples.

After two hours on the bus, I arrived in Himarë. The place that I booked in Himarë is a camping site since all other options were not available on booking.com, unless I wanted to pay more for a hotel. The camping site is called Camping Himara and it’s not too far from Livadi Beach. I had to cycle about 2 miles to get there from the bus stop in Himarë.

The camping site has a bar area. I actually liked the place since it’s on a hill and has a great view.

I went down to the beach only to see that it’s not a sandy beach, but full of little rocks and pebbles. Plus, there were so many umbrellas and glamping tents that I felt a very touristy vibe. Since I’m traveling solo, I didn’t feel like renting an umbrella and chill on the beach by myself. I only stayed for about ten minutes before walking back to the campsite.

If I had known that I didn’t really like the beach I would have stayed on the bus all the way to Sarandë. No use to worry about past mistakes.

I spent the rest of the day chatting with some guests who were also staying at the campground. I also noticed my back tire was leaking air at the base of the valve. I fixed that. I also adjusted the tension on the carbon belt since it needed tightening.

I thought hard about whether to ride my bike to Sarandë the next day or get scammed again and take the bus there. I decided to ride my bike even though I have to ride 36 miles and go over two mountain passes.

Yesterday morning, I started my ride at sunrise. The first major hill was at 12 miles mark. I had to push my bike at certain points because I just didn’t have the energy to ride up the hill. By the time I reached the other side I drank all my water. Luckily, there was a small market and I bought some water for the next big hill. Usually, I don’t need a refill at all when I ride, but this day was different because of the hills.

The scenery was fantastic when I was up in the mountains. I could see a town underneath me and the sea. The Albanian riviera is fantastic!

As I came to another market, I decided to refill my water bottles again and eat a byrek, which is a Balkan pastry with stuffing inside. I chose the meat stuffing because I needed the protein. The other options were spinach or cheese.

The downhills were the dangerous part where I had to be very careful. I was squeezing my brake levers most of the time as there were hairpin turns. For the last 15 miles or so to Sarandë, the road was either slightly downhill or flat. With the mountains to my left side, I had a blissful time coming to the city limit of Sarandë.

In Sarandë, the traffic was bad since it was around 10:30 AM when I arrived. The cops were directing traffic badly as if they didn’t know anything about traffic patterns. Finally, after 36 miles, two large hills, and 4:45 hours of riding, I reached Mega Hostel, the place where I’ll be spending four nights.

I was so sweaty and tired that I didn’t do anything except eating lunch and dinner at nearby restaurants, then taking a shower at the hostel. I ended up going to sleep at around 7 PM.

This morning, since the temperature was cooler, I took a stroll to Sarandë Promenade. The beach there is also a pebble beach, which I didn’t like. At the ferry booth, I bought a ticket to Corfu, Greece, for €37, on Thursday morning at 10 AM. This price includes the €5 bicycle fare.

I don’t know what else to do in Sarandë. It’s the last Albanian town that I’m stay at. There are boat tour to other points of interest if I choose to do that. To be honest, I just want to relax and not do too much.

title: Days 64 and 65: Levan to Vlorë, then a Rest Day in Vlorë
content:
My last night in Levan was terrible. There was no AC so it was very hot in the room with only one small fan. Someone rang the doorbell at midnight for some reason. And there was firework at 1 AM. I don’t know what they were celebrating, but at least it was short lived.

Soon after I started my ride the next morning, it started to rain. My weather app didn’t even forecast rain. I pulled aside to a cafe and had a cup of Albanian coffee, which is served in a shot glass, similar to an espresso.

A local Albanian guy and I started chatting. He was very kind, like many Albanian people. We didn’t talk too much, but he was impressed by my bike tour. In the end, he ended up paying for my coffee. What a generous guy!

I only had to ride 16 miles to Vlorë from Levan and I was glad for that. As I got closer to town, the view was magnificent when I cruised down the hill. There are mountains on the sides and the town is tucked right in the valley where the Ionian Sea and the Adriatic Sea meet. Unfortunately, I didn’t take any photos since I was going downhill so fast.

I arrived at Nana Hostel at 7:30 AM. My clothes were damp from the rain. The owner of the hostel, who is an old lady named Nana, did my laundry. She was so bossy to the other guests and refused to keep the AC on for long so she can save money. She also didn’t provide shampoo to any guests. Not that I needed any. I found her to be the highlight of my stay in Vlorë.

I didn’t do much yesterday afternoon and only rode my bike to get dinner at an Asian restaurant called Nishiki. It’s a mom-and-pop restaurant and the food was so good.

This morning, I rode my bike to the bus station to ask about a bus to Himarë since I don’t want to ride my bike up a giant hill from Vlorë to Himarë tomorrow. The guy assured me that there’s a bus at 7 AM that can take my bike. I hope he’s right.

I did all my Vlorë sightseeing in the morning. There isn’t too much to see. I saw the Independence Monument then rode my bike to Lungomare Beach. The temperature gets hotter later in the day so I came back to the hostel around 10:30.

I spent rest of the morning and most of the afternoon coding a website that will combine my web development portfolio with my photography portfolio and adding a blogging feature. When I’m done bike touring Europe, I will start blogging my next adventure using that website since it doesn’t rely on Google services and might work in China if I decide to go there.

Right now, I feel I’m done cycling. I might even take the bus from Himarë to Sarandë, then take the ferry to Corfu, Greece. It’s just too hot and I only ride about 30 miles max per day. I just want to go back home and get some things done on my to-do list. And for some weird reason, I have a feeling that I might get stopped by ICE at the Philadelphia Airport and be detained and deported. My mind thinks too much sometimes.

title: Days 62 and 63: Durrës to Divjakë, then to Levan
content:
Yesterday morning, I woke up at 5:10 and got on the road at the time of the sunrise, 5:35 AM.

I was glad to be out of the Backpackers Hostel in Durrës because the place was messy and had no AC. I also didn’t have a good vibe there. It was a complete switch from the Mosaic Home hostel in Tiranë, where it was one of the best hostels I’ve stayed at.

In any case, I rode on a service road next to the main highway most of the way. The route followed the EuroVelo the entire time. I reached Olive Guesthouse (Fori Vodo) in Divjakë around 9 AM after riding 35 miles. The owners are an old couple. They were very nice and offered me coffee and some watermelon slices. I stayed in a private room and it had AC. What a wonderful delight!

I didn’t do much in Divjakë because it’s a small town. Except for going out for lunch and dinner I mainly rested in the room and took a nap.

Google somehow flagged my website as “malicious” so it was down for a day. That was a good excuse for me to not write a blog post yesterday. After I disputed it, this website is up again.

This made me think if I care enough about blogging my travels. I mainly do it to remember my adventures. Maybe I should consider moving my blog to WordPress or something other than Blogger if Google gives me any more issues.

This morning, I continued my bicycle journey by following the EuroVelo. I saw some half finished houses on the sides of the road. There were some goats and geese, too. It felt like I went back in time, seeing old bicycles and old cars on the road.

This is the typical Albania I’ve been witnessing the entire time while traveling in this country. Not to say there aren’t any rich people in the country, I did see a new Bentley in Tiranë and some modern BMWs. But the majority of the people own 20+ years old cars or ride on old bicycles that look like they are about to fall apart. My bike must look like a Cadillac to them.

To me, it’s not the material wealth that matters anyway. The Albanian people I’ve met have been very kind and generous. They are the type of people I would like to live with.

After riding 28 miles to Levan, I arrived at Kappa Guesthouse. The lady just finished cleaning and I was able to check-in right away.

Levan is even smaller than Divjakë with only a few stores and restaurants. The owner of the guesthouse had to work at the restaurant where I had my lunch.

My room doesn’t have AC, only a fan. The temperature in the afternoon is now 35C, or 95F. I plan on going out one more time to get dinner. Tomorrow I’ll ride to Vlorë and stay there for two nights since it’s a bigger town.

title: Days 59 to 61: Tiranë to Durrës, then Two Days in Durrës
content:
Before I left Tiranë, I met another long distance cyclist at the hostel. His name is Johannes and he’s from Germany. We had dinner together and it was nice talking to another cyclist. Johannes started from Germany and is making a loop around the Balkans before going back home to start his job in September.

The next morning, I started my ride to Durrës at 5:30. I mainly cycled along a service road that ran parallel to the main road. When I reached the Backpackers Hostel in Durrës I had ridden about 26 miles.

There isn’t much to do in Durrës. In the afternoon, I walked to The Venetian Tower of Durrës, Durrës Amphitheater, and the Byzantine Forum. None of them impressed me. Once I went to Rome, no ruins are worth seeing.

In the hostel, I met a Chinese guy named Qu. We hung out the next day and walked to Durrës Beach. Surprisingly, it’s the only Balkan beach that I’ve been to that has sand. But the temperature was so hot that we only stayed for about an hour before taking a taxi back to the hostel.

There’s another Chinese woman who arrived at the hostel yesterday. Her English name is Teresa. The three of us might grab dinner together tonight. I plan on leaving at 5:30 tomorrow morning to cycle to Divjakë so I have to sleep early tonight.

title: Days 54 to 58: Five Days in Tiranë
content:
I spent five days in Tiranë, the capital of Albania. The first couple of days I hung out with a Dutch girl named Lotte and a Turkish guy named Ismail from the hostel.

We had lunch together and walked to the square in the middle of the city. We also went to Bunk’Art 2, which I thought would be an art gallery of some sort, but it’s about the history of Albania during WWII. There is also the Pyramid of Tirana that I climbed to the top to see some views.

A couple of days later, I rode my bicycle to Dajti Ekspres station and took the cable car to the top of Dajti Mountain. It had great views of the city, but not much to do there.

The past couple of days were very hot. I basically chilled at the hostel and chatted with two Chinese travelers. One is a 21 years old film student who doesn’t have an English name so I’ll call him Gao. The other traveler is in his early 30s and has been traveling on and off for ten years. His English name is Ruke. I haven’t spoken that much Chinese in a long time. It was good to talk to them.

Albania is one of the cheaper countries to stay at. The hostel is only €11 per night. I guess I picked a good country to stay for a month.

Tomorrow, I’ll cycle to Durrës. It’ll be about 26 miles and I hope to get there early in the day.

title: Day 53: Lezhë to Tiranë
content:
This morning, I left Vila Kastriotet-Hotel at 5:30 and rode about 43 miles to Tiranë. It took me about four and half hours with a rest stop for a soft drink at a gas station.

I was finally honked at by an Albanian driver when I was trying to navigate a roundabout. I guess I was just supposed to cut in rather than wait for the cars to go pass. In any case, the drivers in Eastern Europe have been very patient with me and this was certainly an exception.

I arrived at the Mosaic Home hostel in Tiranë a little before 10 AM and waited until 1 PM to check in. After settling down and taking a shower, I went on the hunt for some ramen since I haven’t had any Asian food in a while.

The first ramen restaurant I went to was 30 minutes away by walking. I was disappointed to find out that the ramen restaurant only offered instant ramen that the customer had to cook. It reminded me of the Seinfeld episode when Kramer tried to sell his make-your-own-pizza idea. I didn’t want to eat instant ramen so I only bought a boba tea there.

I walked along the lake in the Tirana Lake Park before finding another noodle shop called Kungfu Noodle Bar. This time, I had some delicious noodles.

I’m back at the hostel now. Realistically, I think Tiranë is only worth two or three days of exploration. Since I have plenty of time before getting to Greece on August 13 I plan on staying in Tiranë for about 5 or 6 days before moving on to Durrës.

title: Day 52: Shkodër to Lezhë
content:
Yesterday afternoon, I had the honor of putting my handprints on the wall at Chuck and Susan’s place. I made my handprints look like little feet as that’s something I didn’t see anyone do. What can I say, I like to be different.

I fell asleep early and didn’t get a chance to properly say goodbye to Chuck and Susan. But I’m so glad that I was hosted by them. They are legends in the Warmshowers community and it’s definitely one of the highlights of my trip.

This morning, I left their apartment at 5:30 to start my ride to Lezhë. The route on Organic Maps took me on the major road, SH1, for most of the time. The morning traffic was light. Then I turned to a gravel path with tall plants on both sides of me. I didn’t like it so much since it felt like I was riding in a jungle. When I reached a more rural road I was glad there was pavement and fewer cars. Eventually, I returned to SH1 and rode into Lezhë. I arrived at Vila Kastriotet-Hotel around 8 AM after riding 26.7 miles.

After checking in at 10 AM, I took a shower then walked around the town. There were only a few things to see, the Skanderbeg Tomb and Lezhë Castle. I opted not to hike up the hill to Lezhë Castle and only walked around the site of the Skanderbeg Tomb. I didn’t think much of it and didn’t pay the 200 LEK to go inside.

Back in the hotel room, I learned that Heinz Stücke passed away three days ago on July 22. He’s the cyclist who bicycled around the world continuously for over 50 years. I met him last year and admired him greatly because he lived a life that he chose, not based on what society determined. He’s a legend who influenced many cyclists. May he rest in peace.

I’ve had a lot of time to think and reflect on my life and life in general. I feel very happy and content right now. I have everything I need. When I get back home I will downsize more. Life on a bicycle made me appreciate all the things I carry. My mind is satisfied and I’m physically healthy. What more can I ask. I also have to remind myself that nothing is as good as it is and nothing is as bad as it is. Follow the Middle Way. And be grateful for what I have and what I’m experiencing.

title: Days 46 to 51: Six More Days in Shkodër
content:
I stayed at Chuck and Susan’s apartment for another six days, making a total of nine days. Chuck told me that I’m now tied for the longest stays at their place. I’m very grateful that they allowed to me stay this long. Previously, I thought about getting a hostel, but Chuck extended his invitation.

I did some chores around the apartment, including sweeping the patio, taking down two doors, and sharpening some knives. I also cleaned my bicycle and donated a few things from my panniers for future cyclists.

Shkodër reminds me of Asia with all the bicycles. Albania is still a developing country with the occasional water outages that happened in the past few days as they are still trying to complete the city’s infrastructure.

Overall, I had a great time in Shkodër. It was definitely a change of pace going from cycling to a more slow-down life. Tomorrow, I’ll resume cycling and ride 26 miles south to Lezhë.

title: Days 42 to 45: Two Rest Days in Shkodër and a Hike from Valbonë to Theth
content:
As it turned out, only one cyclist showed up a few days ago. Her name is Niamh and she’s from the United Kingdom. Her front tire got a puncture while coming here so she spent some time finding a new tire in town. The following day, we cycled to the nearby lake town of Shiroka and chilled on the bank for a bit before cycling back.

Niamh told me about the hike she did the last time she was in Albania. It was organized by her hostel, The Wanderers Hostel. The hike is six hours long from Valbonë to Theth. There’s also a separate hike to a waterfall and a pool called the Blue Eye in Theth. I decided to sign up with the hostel. So for the past two nights I was in the Albanian Alps.

The trip to Valbonë took about seven hours from Shkodër. It consisted of a bus ride to Koman, a ferry to Fierzë, then a minibus ride to the Adenisi Guest House.

Since the trip was organized by the hostel, everybody knew each other beforehand except me. I tried to be social, but still felt ostracized since everyone was in their early twenties and most of them were paired already, either as couples or as friends.

In any case, I took a nap at the hostel and didn’t even eat lunch. The dinner provided by the guest house was too shy on the meats and I only had one chicken leg as the protein. However, I did pack three boiled eggs, along with a few other things, for the hike the next morning.

The hostel manager drove us to the trailhead and we started hiking around 6:30 AM. It took me two hours to hike to the top of the mountain then about 3.5 hours down to Guesthouse Dreni in Theth. The view was great, but on the way down I slipped several time since I didn’t hike with hiking shoes, just regular walking shoes. There were some cafes along the hiking route but I kept going.

I was one of the first few hikers from the group to reach the hostel in Theth. Apparently, I would have been the first one if the people before me didn’t catch a ride.

This guesthouse had a buffet style dinner and I ate a full meal by the time I went to bed. I slept for almost 12 hours last night.

This morning, I opted not to do the hike to the waterfall and Blue Eye because yesterday’s hike was the longest hike I’ve ever done in my life. I simply didn’t want to hike anymore, so I took the minibus back to Shkodër.

When I arrived back at Chuck and Susan’s place I met a German couple and a French couple. I didn’t quite catch any of their names since they are all busy doing something.

I really don’t know what to do for the next several days. According to my current plan, I  will stay in Shkodër for six more nights before cycling farther south.

title: Days 40 and 41: Budva to Bar, then to Shkodër, Albania
content:
Yesterday, I started my ride from Budva at the usual time of 5:30 AM. I cycled on the main road most of the time and the occasional side roads. At one point, I had to push my bike up a steep hill with switchbacks. The hill was so steep that I had to stop and rest on every turn so my calves can get a break. Even though the journey was only 23.5 miles to Bar, it took me three hours to get to Sova Smart House hostel.

I was able to self check-in, but I still had to wait for the hostel manager to show up so I can pay. As I was waiting, another guest showed up. Her name is Kristen and she’s a 36 years old makeup artist from California. We hit it off right away.

Kristen loves hiking and just spent ten days hiking the Peaks of Balkans trail that connects Albania, Kosovo, and Montenegro. She is also financially independent, but doesn’t realize it yet. We ended up spending the rest of the day together going to the beachside, visiting the Church of St. John Vladimir, and eating lunch.

Talking to her is like talking to a female version of myself. We both feel traveling is our main goal in life and being independent is very important for both of us. Of all the people I met during my travels we have the most in common. I had a blast hanging out with her for a day.

This morning, I started my ride at 5:20 and rode up one more big but gradual hill before coming into Albania. The border crossing was much better this time when the agent waved me to the front of a line of cars so I got processed faster.

I arrived in the city of Shkodër at 9 AM after 32 miles of riding. I’ll be staying at the most famous Warmshowers hosts’ place for tonight. They are an American couple who chose to retire in Albania. They are Chuck and Susan.

Upon entering their apartment, I saw the famous wall of palm prints of all the cyclists who had stayed here. Then I was greeted by Susan, Chuck’s wife. Over a glass of iced water, Chuck and I chatted about what to expect while stay at their place. I learned that him and Susan have hosted almost 1600 cyclists in the past seven years. That’s just amazing!

For lunch, I ate at Chuck and Susan’s favorite restaurant, Puri. I ordered the Father’s Rice meal and it was THE meal for a long distance cyclist, with rice, meat, beans, and salad.

I’m now back at Chuck and Susan’s apartment. There will be three more cyclists coming in today. It’ll be a very lively group of people here for the night.

I plan to stay in Albania for a month, but I don’t know how many days I want to stay in Shkodër and where. I’ll decide on that soon.

title: Day 39: Herceg Novi to Budva
content:
This morning, I woke up at 4:45 and got on the road at 5:30.

The first part of the route was easy as I cycled along the coast on the promenade. Then I took the free ferry, at least it’s free for cyclists, from Kamenari to Lepetani so I didn’t have cycle around the inner Bay of Kotor. For the rest of the way to Budva I was on the E80, which is the only road to Budva. Luckily, the road has two lanes going each direction despite the fact that the right lane is being worked on. I felt safe for the most part even though the road felt like a highway.

When I turned off E80 I saw a cafe called Caffe Firma and I decided to get something to eat. As soon as I parked my bike it started to rain out of nowhere. I was glad of my decision and spent about an hour at the cafe eating an omelette along with a cup of coffee and avoided the rain.

There was a Syrian guy who saw me and immediately started speaking Mandarin to me. I was so shocked that he spoke fluent Chinese. He had lived in China for 15 years and seemed to like it there very much. It was a delight for me to practice my Mandarin with him in a small cafe in Montenegro, of all places.

When the rain died down, I cycled up one big hill. On the way down I had to be extra careful and not to go too fast since the road was wet and there were some hairpin turns. I heard my back wheel slid on one of the sharp turns but I didn’t crash. I really hate going downhills with sharp turns when the ground is wet. When I reached the bottom of the hill I arrived at the Newborn Hostel after riding 25 miles from Herceg Novi.

While waiting to check in, I chatted with some travelers. There were three guys who were hitchhiking to Dubrovnik. They are definitely the freewheeling type of guys who don’t even know where to spend the night and letting the journey decide for them.

I also met a traveler named Adrian. He’s from Poland and is 29 years old. After checking in, we decided to walk to the old town together. We visited Church of Saint John the Baptist, Citadela Budva, and the Budva ballerina sculpture.

I feel like I was talking to myself because Adrian and I have so much in common. We have similar beliefs about life, money, and freedom. Adrian works as a freelance logistics manager and wants to be financially independent by the age of 35. I recommended the book that I’m currently reading, The Art of Spending Money, since he also read The Psychology of Money by the same author.

There weren’t much to see in Budva after visiting the old town so we came back to the  hostel. Adrian and I might meet up again for dinner. After that I will get some sleep. Tomorrow there will be more hills, but only 23 miles to Bar. I plan on doing the same thing, waking up around sunrise and start my ride early.

title: Day 38: Dubrovnik to Herceg Novi, Montenegro
content:
Last night, or rather late afternoon, I went to bed around 6 PM so I can wake up at dawn to get ready for the 33 mile ride to Herceg Novi, Montenegro.

I started my ride just at the time of the sunrise, around 5:20. There were some hills going out of Dubrovnik and I had to carry my bike over a guard rail to get on the main road. The morning traffic was a bit busy because I was coming out of a major city. There were a couple of times when large trucks honked at me from behind so I had to pull to the side to get out of the way.

My favorite part of the ride was cycling by some vineyards on my right hand side with the mountains to my left. There was barely any traffic on that road and the cooler temperature made that section of the route very pleasant.

The border control to Montenegro was slow. When it was finally my turn, the guard waved me through without stamping my passport. I told him that I will return to the Schengen zone in Greece so I need him to stamp or scan my passport. He reluctantly scanned it and was kind of annoyed at me. I hope when I enter Greece in about a month everything will be fine.

Finally, I had left Schengen and entered Montenegro. The last four miles to my guesthouse was on the Pet Danica Seaside Promenade. People were hanging out on the beaches and shops began to open. I had to be careful not to run into the pedestrians. A little after 9 AM, I arrived at Zemunella Guest House in Herceg Novi.

After checking in, I had a seafood pasta for lunch on the promenade. Then I went to find a beach spot to dip my feet into the water.

On one of the beaches, I saw a bicycle loaded with panniers. Sure enough, there was a guy sunbathing. I asked him if he’s bicycle touring. Unfortunately, he didn’t speak English, only Czech. We communicated via Google Translate and he told me that he doesn’t stay in hostels or hotels, only camping. That’s not my way of bike touring. Since he didn’t speak English, I ditched the idea of seeking him as a bike touring companion.

I walked back to the guesthouse and took a shower. I will eat dinner soon before sleeping early again.

Tomorrow, I will ride 25 miles to Budva and stick to the coastal route from Organic Maps. My Warmshowers host in Shkodër, Albania, warned me about the traffic and provided me with a GPX route that goes inland. But that route has hills and it will take me a day longer to get to Shkodër. I decided that if I cycle early in the morning there will be less traffic. Let’s hope for the best.

title: Days 36 and 37: Ferry from Split to Dubrovnik, then Rest Day in Dubrovnik
content:
Yesterday, I spent more time in Split by walking around the old town. I bought the ferry ticket for €50 for myself then paid €25 for the bicycle once I boarded the catamaran. The entire trip to Dubrovnik was over 5 hours with several stops in between. After arriving at the port at 8:20 PM, I cycled about a mile to Hostel Hakuna Matata and arrived before the sunset. As soon as I checked in I went to bed.

This morning, I woke up at 6 then walked about 20 minutes to the old town in Dubrovnik. I was glad I went there early to avoid the crowd, but most places weren’t open yet. I saw the Lovrjenac Fortress outside the city walls before walking inside the walls to old town.

Like many other cities in Croatia that I’ve been to, the streets are narrow. I didn’t feel many people live there since so many restaurants and cafes catered to tourists. I wanted to walk on the walls of the old town but I needed to pay €40 for a ticket. I decided against the idea.

The best way to see the old town is just to wander around. I went inside a couple of churches and took many photographs of the streets. Since old town isn’t that big, I didn’t stay too long and came back to the hostel at 10 AM.

I took a nap then ate a burger for lunch. Tomorrow, I’ll be cycling out of Dubrovnik and out of Croatia into Montenegro.

Overall, the Croatian coast is very beautiful. I love seeing the mountains and the sea in one place. Next time, I’ll do more island hopping and visit the capital, Zagreb.

I missed seeing Pavle, the Croatian traveler I met in Paphos, Cyprus, last year. He lives in Metković. Since I took the ferry from Split to Dubrovnik I missed his town. Maybe I’ll see Pavle next time when I’m in Croatia. However, I did meet David and Ervin in Novigrad. I hope to see them again.

title: Day 35: Trogir to Split
content:
Two nights ago, I didn’t sleep well. My mind was active due to the caffeine I had during the day. I guess two cups of coffee and two Cokes really messed me up. I made some ramen noodles around midnight and ate that before finally falling to sleep at 1 AM.

The next morning, I was up at 4:45. I decided to ride the 17 miles from Trogir to Split rather than taking the ferry. I started at 5:30 and the ride was very enjoyable without many cars on the road. As I got close to the city of Split there were some hills, but nothing major that I couldn’t handle.

I arrived at Hostel Elli at 7 AM. I was too early and waited outside the building for a while before getting a cappuccino at a coffee shop nearby.

When I came back to the hostel, I met two young touring cyclists who were preparing to leave. Their names are Finn and Fin. I think they are both from New Zealand. They were heading for the bus station to take the Flixbus to Dubrovnik. I wondered if the bus would take bicycles. As it turned out, it all depended on the driver. Finn later messaged me on Instagram that they had to change route because the Dubrovnik driver didn’t allow bicycles so they took a different bus to Mostar in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

After getting inside the hostel, I stored my panniers in the kitchen then rode my bike to the bus station to inquire about the bicycle situation. I didn’t see any bike racks on the buses so I guess it really did depend on the driver. I didn’t like the idea of storing my bike in the storage compartment since something can break when the bike is leaned on its side. I decided I would stick to the original idea of taking the ferry to Dubrovnik, which is more expensive than the bus.

It was still early in the day. I walked around the old town in Split, saw the Diocletian’s Palace, and took photos of the Saint Domnius Cathedral. I ate a really good Cevapi sandwich at Kantun Paulina. The sandwich is a pita bread stuffed with sausages, with some kind of a red sauce called ajvar, and onions. So good!

After this much needed meal, I spent a long time hiking up stairs to the top of Forest Park Marjan, where I was rewarded with great views of the sea and the mountains.

I saw everything I wanted to see in Split so I didn’t want to stay an extra night like in my original booking. If I could buy a ferry ticket then I will leave for Dubrovnik today. Unfortunately, all the ferry tickets were sold out for the Krilo line and there’s only the TP line that has a ferry leaving at 3:10 PM. I will buy that ticket this afternoon and hopefully I can take my bike on it. I’ll arrive in Dubrovnik around 8:20 PM.

In the afternoon, I came back to the hostel, checked in, took a shower, did laundry, and planned for my stays for the next few days. After eating some Chinese food at a nearby restaurant I went to bed soon after and slept for almost 11 hours.

Today, I’ll try to take the 3:10 PM ferry and I have plenty of time to do more exploration in Split. Not sure where I want to go, but I have to check out by 10 AM.

title: Day 34: Šibenik to Trogir
content:
After waking up this morning, I had to decide on today’s route to Trogir from Šibenik. There were two options: one is to follow the 32 mile EuroVelo route that partially goes along the coast with many small hills, the other is a 27 mile route that goes inland and slowly climbs a big hill. I chose the second route, thinking that the climb won’t be that bad and I’ll have a good downhill to ride into Trogir.

Sure enough, I kicked myself as I slowly rode up the hill at 5-6 miles per hour. The hill had an incline for about 9 miles. The only good thing about it was the tarmac and there weren’t too many cars early in the morning.

I only rode downhill for a short distance before the route turned into a trail with loose stones. When I saw how steep the downhill was I realized that there was no safe way to ride it with my bike. I had to walk my bicycle carefully while holding both brake levers. What’s worse was the cliff on my right side. I imagined the worst thing happening, which is somehow my bike will slip and fall down the cliff. That’ll be the end of my bike tour for sure.

As I slowly and carefully guided my bike down the gravel hill I wish I had picked the first route. There was a reason that the people behind EuroVelo chose that particular route rather than this shorter one from Organic Maps.

I took several breaks on the path by leaning my bike down on the ground since the kickstand was useless on a steep decline. The view of Trogir was the only good thing about this trail. But there were times when I wanted to throw my bike down the cliff out of frustration so that I didn’t have to suffer on this hill anymore. In the end, my mental strength persevered and my fingers were so sore from holding the brake levers.

The last bit of the trail was a paved road on a residential street. I cycled down the hill and was so worried that my brakes’ stopping power won’t be enough to stop my bike. At the very bottom of the hill when the street came to an intersection with the main road I had to use my feet to stop my bike from going any farther.

That hill was torture, physically and mentally, and I was so glad that I came down it safely. This experience will be inked in my memory for a long time as one of the worst and scariest days of my bike tours. Up there with Hayters Gap in Virginia and the rainy day in Austria.

When I arrived at Hostel Marina Trogir my shirt was soaked with sweat and white salt stains. The owner was able to check me in early and I relaxed in the common area.

Around noon, I had some Thai food in Trogir before exploring the historic old town that’s on an island.

There were only two attractions that were worth seeing, St. Lawrence’s Cathedral and Kamerlengo Castle. I paid the entrance fees with a student discount since I carried my old university ID in my wallet. It works in my advantage when I look ten years younger. I was able to enjoy great panoramic views of the town from top of the bell tower and on top of the castle.

I came back to the hostel soon after and took a shower. I might walk more around the nearby neighborhood then get dinner. Tomorrow, I might ride the 17 miles to Split or take the ferry there if I decide to sleep in. I’ll have to see how I feel. I’m just glad that I got over today’s challenging ride.

title: Day 33: Drage to Šibenik
content:
I didn’t go see the sunset yesterday because I was too tired. The sun was going to set anyway, with or without me.

This morning, I left the guesthouse in Drage before 6 and mainly rode on the D8 route to Šibenik. After 25 miles of cycling, I arrived at Hostel Splendido a little after 8 AM.

I wasn’t surprised that no one was at the reception since it was too early to check-in. I stored my bicycle and panniers upstairs then I walked to the old town.

The streets in Šibenik were narrow and reminded me of the streets in Zadar. I ended up going to the Cathedral of St. James, which has over 70 carved heads on the building. Some of them are of animals, such as a dog or a lion. The ticket to the cathedral also included Civitas Sacra, which is a church museum.

I then walked to the St. Michael’s Fortress, but I didn’t go inside because I didn’t feel like it. That’s the great thing about traveling solo, I get to do whatever I want.

When I came back to the hostel, I chatted with a bicycle tourist who was leaving the hostel. His name is Greg and he doesn’t have any social media accounts and doesn’t document his journey either. I found him interesting because he bought a bicycle in Turkey and will cycle to Italy, then he will just give the bike away. He told me he’s done several bike tours and at the end of his journeys he gives away his bicycle. This gives me the idea of buying a bicycle in Latin America, if I want to cycle tour there, then I’ll give it away at the end. Greg is very free spirited and doesn’t know where he’s staying for the night. He’s also a bit crazy and starts his ride at noon, the hottest time of the day.

After checking in, I took a two hour nap, then showered. I didn’t feel like eating at a restaurant so I went to the grocery store and bought ramen, canned sardines, canned corn, and canned ham. After eating these for dinner I will go to sleep early since I have to ride about 32 miles to Trogir tomorrow. There will be some hills too.

Thank you Croatia for acknowledging cyclists!

title: Days 31 and 32: Veli Lošinj to Mali Lošinj, Ferry to Zadar, then Bike to Drage
content:
Yesterday, I didn’t write because there wasn’t much to write about. I cycled about 30 minutes from Veli Lošinj to Mali Lošinj then took the 9:30 AM ferry to Zadar.

Once in Zadar, I ate a kebab wrap for lunch then checked into The Hostel. I ended up chilling in the dorm for several hours listening to music. In the afternoon I walked around the old town.

I had the best tuna salad I’ve ever had at Fish House Zadar in old town. The tuna meat was cooked so well. I wish I had taken a photo of it.

In any case, there is a Roman forum and a couple of churches in old town. The best part of Zadar, to me, was the Sea Organ. It’s a music instrument mounted beneath a staircase and played by the waves on the sea. I’ve never seen anything like it before. Next to it is The Greeting to the Sun that consists of solar panels and plays a light show at night. So cool!

I also waited for the sunset by the shore. There were so many people doing the same that as soon as the sun had set, I walked back to the hostel.

This morning, I started my ride at 6:30 to Drage, about 23 miles south of Zadar. I had planned on staying at a campsite that’s owned by a Warmshowers host, but I decided to book a guesthouse instead so I can stay cool indoors. Plus, I didn’t know what I would do at a campsite for the whole day.

I arrived at Bed & Breakfast Drage guesthouse around 9 AM. After checking in, I relaxed and did some reading inThe Art of Spending Money. I feel like the author and I have the same mindset about money. The book just reaffirms what I already believe.

In the afternoon, I walked to the beach part of Drage and had a seafood pasta for lunch. When I came back to my room I tried to build and deploy my home inventory manager app that I had built six months ago on my MacBook laptop. After a few hours of trying, I was able to make it work only for my computer, but not on any other macOS due to a signing issue and the application file being too large to host on Github. In the end, I was too tired and hungry so I gave up.

I just had some seafood pizza for dinner. I plan to walk to a lookout point not far from the guesthouse where I can see another sunset. Tomorrow, I’ll ride about 25 miles to Šibenik and stay at a hostel. I hope to get there around 9 AM to avoid the heat and the traffic.

title: Days 29 and 30: Two Rest Days in Veli Lošinj
content:
I spent the past two days just relaxing at the hostel and going to the beach. Nothing too interesting, but I’m glad to have spend some alone time so that I can do some thinking.

I planned my destinations ahead so that I can leave the Schengen area from Croatia and return to the Schengen in Greece on time for my flight back to Philadelphia. I’ll be spending about a month in Montenegro and Albania since they are not in the Schengen zone.

I also watched some YouTube videos about cycling and traveling, then I did administration work on the computer.

Today, I borrowed an ebook calledThe Art of Spending Money by Morgan Housel. I read Morgan’s previous books so I hope this book will be interesting as well.

I thought about what I should do after I get back home. After voting in the midterm election in November, I will do some slow traveling in Latin America. Maybe I’ll complete a CELTA certification so I can teach English in foreign countries. Another option is to get a certificate in project management and pursue a corporate job, which is something I’m more hesitant to do.

The temperature has gotten a little cooler. At least it’s not in the 30C anymore, but the humidity makes it still feel hotter.

Tomorrow, I will take the 9:30 AM ferry from Mali Lošinj to Zadar. I will explore the town in the afternoon and spend a night at a hostel before cycling down the Croatian coast again.

title: Day 28: Ferry from Pula to Mali Lošinj, then Bike to Veli Lošinj
content:
After writing my previous blog post, I went to get some dinner and saw the Temple of Augustus in Pula. To be honest, after visiting Rome nothing really compares.

Hostel Antique is a very nice hostel and I enjoyed the air conditioning in the kitchen area and in the dorm. I ended up going to sleep around 7 PM and woke up at 5:15 AM.

I only cycled about a mile to the ferry terminal and arrived an hour early. The ferry to Mali Lošinj wasn’t canceled and the boat ride took about 2:20 hours to the island of Lošinj.

When I arrived at the port of Mali Lošinj, it was already hot. I had to pedal another 4 miles to the HI Hostel in the village of Veli Lošinj, going up some hills.

At 10 AM, I finally reached the hostel. However, the place looked empty. No receptionist, no guests. I waited for an hour inside and finally the receptionist and the cleaning lady saw me. It turned out they had closed the hostel temporarily for cleaning and weren’t expecting any guests. I was the last guest who booked the hostel on booking.com before they closed it. Lucky for me, they allowed me to stay at the hostel even though I’ll be the only guest in the entire place.

The ferry service, Krilo, informed me that the Friday ferry from Mali Lošinj to Zadar has been canceled. Looks like I need to stay for two more nights in the hostel and get on the Saturday morning ferry. This is unexpected. Such is the nature of an adventure.

I wish I was staying at a more social hostel. I don’t know what to do for the next two days. Mali Lošinj is a small village with few restaurants. There is a beach that I will go to today. That’s about all there is in this place. I’ll be very bored. Maybe this is a good thing. I get to do some reflecting.

Last night was so hot. The dorm doesn’t have air conditioning. The receptionist loaned me a fan and it worked ok. I can’t believe I’m stuck on an island in Croatia. But there are worse things in the world.

title: Day 27: Rovinj to Pula
content:
Yesterday afternoon, I walked around the town of Rovinj. It was the hottest part of the day and didn’t have the will to go up to see the bell tower. I did have an excellent tuna poke bowl for dinner at Fish House Rovinj though. When I got back to the studio apartment, I thought about going to see the sunset in a couple of hours. Then my body told me it’s time to sleep so I went to bed around 7 PM.

This morning, I left the apartment at 5:45. I followed the EuroVelo 8 route again and it took me to some trails with rough terrain and rocks. I don’t know what I dislike more, uphills or rocky trails.

Since I only had to ride about 23 miles I arrived at Hostel Antique in Pula at 9 AM. I couldn’t check in because I was so early, but I was able to store my bicycle on the ground floor and my panniers in the storage room. I paid €12 to do laundry, which was quite expensive considering I only have three sets of clothing to wash.

I took this time to eat a salad for breakfast, walked around the town, and bought a ferry ticket for tomorrow morning to Mali Lošinj, a small town on an island farther south. I might have to stay there for two nights since the next ferry to Zadar will be on Friday, unless I want to take a different ferry that will arrive in Zadar on Thursday night at almost midnight. Not sure if I want to arrive so late.

After checking into the hostel, my laundry was done too. I went out again to get some lunch then came back and applied for some Workaway volunteering opportunities in Albania, took a shower, and napped.

In Pula, I’ve already seen the Arch of the Sergii, Pula Arena, and the Pula Citadel. I missed the Temple of Augustus so I will go see that after writing this post. Then I will eat dinner and probably call it a day. Tomorrow, I’ll take the 7 AM ferry to Mali Lošinj, unless it gets canceled due to the wind and the rain. We’ll have to see.

title: Day 26: Novigrad to Rovinj
content:
After writing my previous blog post, I ended up walking around the town center of Novigrad and met up with Ervin at the Fish Food Bila stand for dinner. Ervin was so nice and paid for my fish and chips meal.

We chatted about our family backgrounds. Ervin has three half siblings and one step sister. He’s working as an interior designer and furniture maker.

After dinner we got some drinks at a bar and sat outside. Soon, David showed up. He didn’t go to the concert after all. We had a great time conversing about the 90s since the music at the bar were all hits from that era. It was very easy to talk to these guys about anything. We really hit it off! After a brief visit by a friend of theirs, I had to go back to the guesthouse since it was getting late. I didn’t go to bed until 10:45 PM.

I made sure to wake up early today, at 4:30, so I can book a place in Rovinj. I ended up getting a studio apartment near the center of the town. It’s unusual that I booked something on the day of, but I was indecisive.

I left the guesthouse in Novigrad at 5:30. The ride today was full of variety. It included riding along the coast, on the road, on the gravel path, in the woods, on rough terrain, down a steep hill, then up a steep hill, next to cars, and in insolation.

There was a long stretch where the ground was so bumpy with rocks that I felt like I was mountain biking. There were actually two mountain bikers riding the same trail as me.

But the worst was the steep hill that I had to cycle up. It was just steep enough that I could pedal with the lowest gear. Very slowly, at about 4 miles per hour. There were cars, trucks, RVs, and buses on the same road as me. Given no shoulder to cycle on, I was very glad that the drivers in Croatia were careful enough to wait and then go around me. After about two miles of uphill, I surprised myself that I cycled the entire thing without pushing my bike.

It was a tough day. After 39 miles, I finally made it to the Studio App Lenny apartment at 11 AM. Checking in was a bit difficult because the host didn’t reply to me quickly enough as I was sweating outside trying to figure out how to store my bike. I ended up putting my bike in the room on the ground floor.

When I brought my panniers up to the apartment, I saw that one of the screws had broken off the plastic railing that holds the handle. Without it, it’ll be a matter of time when the next screw breaks off. Then my pannier wouldn’t be able to attach to the rack. I can’t believe I had to fix something again. Yesterday, I rigged an outlet adapter and today I have to fix this hole.

I ended up securing a zip tie to the hole since the end of the zip tie is just big enough that it acted as a plug. I’m curious to see how long this fix will last.

Inside the apartment, I relaxed, made some ramen for lunch, and took a shower. It’s past 5 PM. I plan to explore the town a little then get dinner. Tomorrow won’t be as hard as today. No major hills and only about 23 miles to Pula.

title: Day 25: Piran to Novigrad, Croatia
content:
This morning, I woke up at 5 AM and started my ride at 5:30. Rather than going the most direct way to Novigrad, Croatia, I followed the EuroVelo 8 route that took me mainly along the coast of the Istrian Peninsula. The Istrian Peninsula is the northwestern part of Croatia. Part of it includes Slovenia and a little bit of Italy.

The ride was about 37 miles in total. I stopped by a couple of places. At the first cafe, I had a banana split and a cappuccino for breakfast. Then at the Skybar cafe, about 1.5 miles away from Novigrad, I had a fruit smoothie.

After drinking my smoothie, just when I was about to get on my bike, a young man asked me about my bicycle. I ended up staying a bit longer to chat with him and his friend about bike touring.

The young man’s name is David and his friend’s name is Ervin. They are both 35 years old and are locals born in Novigrad. David asked me all kinds of questions about touring bicycles and what to look for when buying one. I also told him about my past bike tours and wish I had started an around the world bike tour when I was younger, maybe at David’s age.

Since I’m 42 now, I’m more picky about my accommodations and prefer hostels and hotels rather than wild camping. I tend to eat at restaurants rather than going into a grocery store and cook something for myself. To be honest, I don’t think I have the mentality to ride a bicycle around the world anymore now that I’m so picky. I think there’s a bit of wildness when you are younger, and you can tolerate harsher conditions due to your naivety, or stupidity.

I rode into Novigrad with David and Ervin after our initial meeting. Ervin had to go to work so David and I cycled to the town square and had some orange juice. David invited to see David Byrne of the Talking Heads tonight in Pula, a town south of here, about an hour away by car. It’ll be a late night if I go. Most likely, I’ll stay in.

Around noon, I parted ways with David at the Pansion Comfort Santa Marija guesthouse, where I’ll be staying for the night. I was able to check-in at noon since my room was ready.

After a pasta lunch, I bought some newspapers because I decided that I would cut my hair in my room. Since I had bought a hair clipper back when I was in Ottawa, Canada, I’m going to use it to cut my hair. The newspaper is to catch the hair on the floor.

Everything was going well during the cut until the battery in my clipper went out. But I still had some hairs to cut. The clipper charger has a North American style plug and I don’t have an international adapter. My other plug is the Apple adapters set that only works on USB-C cables. Unfortunately, the clipper has a different type of connector.

I asked the receptionist of the guesthouse to see if she has an adapter. She found some international plugs, but missing the part where the plug goes in. I also messaged my newly made friends, David and Ervin, to see if they had any international adapters. They did not. I even biked to a gas station to see if they sell an international adapter. Nope.

I wondered how weird I’d be if I rode my bike tomorrow with my head half shaved. I’ll definitely be making a funny statement.

Then I thought, maybe I can rig one of the plugs that the receptionist gave me by removing some plastics by the contacts on the input so that the prongs on my clipper’s charger can touch them to get electricity. And that’s what I did with the pliers on my multi-tool. I snapped off some plastics on the adapter and carefully held the charger to the contacts and it worked! I was able to charge my hair clipper.

Funny thing is, after I cut the rest of my hair and took a shower, I noticed there’s a hand vacuum for shavers in the bathroom that took the exact plug type that I needed for the hair clipper. Only if I had looked carefully!

What an adventure it was to get my haircut. That was the highlight of the day. Now, I’m clean, refreshed, and didn’t electrocute myself.

The guesthouse has a free breakfast in the morning, but I’ll be leaving early again. The chef packed a meal for me, which I’m very grateful.

Not sure what I’ll do for the rest of the day. Maybe I’ll meet with Ervin for dinner.

I have to book my accommodation for tomorrow night at the town of Rovinj. It’s the high season and I can’t find cheaper places to stay. It really sucks when I have to pay around $100 for a night.

title: Day 24: Train from Ljubljana to Koper, then Bike to Piran
content:
After writing my blog post yesterday, I met a new roommate named Oliver. He’s a young lad from Russia and suffered memory loss from a boxing match recently. I surely don’t want to be in his shoes. The dorm was full last night and apparently I was snoring too loud. I didn’t even notice.

This morning, I woke up at 5:15 and got to the train station around 6 AM. The train to Koper was supposed to leave at 6:45, but it stayed on the tracks for an hour.

I got very lucky when someone told me that the train will split with one half going to Koper and the other half going to Rijeka, Croatia. I had put my bicycle in the wrong train car. That would have been bad if my bicycle went to Rijeka and I went to Koper. My trip would have been a mess if that happened.

The train ride took forever because it kept on stopping randomly on the tracks. I didn’t get to Koper until 11:10 AM.

After I got my bike down from the train, I told myself that I would never take the bike on a train again in Slovenia. Such a nightmare.

Since the train arrived late, now I have to ride about 13 miles to Piran in the heat. Luckily, most of it was on a bike path.

I took refuge in Izola, which is a town at the half way point, and had myself a kebab wrap for lunch. Then I cycled the rest of the way to Piran.

I checked into Hostel Adriatic Piran at 1 PM. While resting in the hostel kitchen, I chatted with two French travelers, Laure and Gauttier. Laure told me about her Workaway experience in Slovenia. I’m considering doing a Workaway in Albania so it was nice to get some information. Gauttier and Laure were so kind that they even offered me some watermelons. Much appreciated!

For the rest of the afternoon, I walked around the town. Not much to see except for Tartini Square and Church of St. George.

The heat was scorching and I tried to walk under the shades of the buildings. Even then I was sweating profusely. I had an octopus salad as an early dinner before coming back to the hostel and taking a shower.

I booked a rather expensive accommodation for tomorrow for $105 at the town of Novigrad, Croatia. I had a couple of options, including wild camping and a poorly rated hostel. I decided to keep myself sane in this heat by treating myself. I will leave in the early morning again tomorrow.

title: Days 22 and 23: Train from Maribor to Ljubljana, then a Rest Day in Ljubljana
content:
Yesterday morning, I left Tatjana’s place early because she had a cleaning lady over. I arrived at the Maribor train station hours before my departure so I took my time and had a kebab wrap for breakfast.

The train to Ljubljana arrived on time at 11:35 AM. However, the platform for the train was about three feet above the platform of the station. Luckily, there were other cyclists getting on the same train and one of them helped me get my bike on the train.

After about three hours, I arrived in Ljubljana. There is some major renovations at the station and I had to push my bike up a flight of stairs. The bike ramp was too narrow since I also have panniers on my bike. Again, another lady helped me by lifting the back wheel so I could move my bike up the stairs. I’m so grateful for the kindness of strangers!

I rode less than two miles to the Guesthouse GreenSLO hostel and I was so sweaty by the time I arrived. Due to heat, I only went out for an early dinner then came back to the hostel.

This morning, I woke up before 6 AM and cycled into Ljubljana city center then walked around to do some exploration of my own.

Even though Ljubljana is the capital of Slovenia, it’s very walkable. I went to Metelkova, which is full of houses covered in graffiti. After parking my bike by a park, I walked to the Three Bridge, the Dragon Bridge, Central Market, Town Square, Plečnik House, National and University Library, Republic Square, and Tivoli Park. I opted not to walk up the steep hill to Ljubljana Castle. It would be too much walking for me.

I was glad that I did most of my exploration in the morning to avoid the heat, but most attractions didn’t open until later. After eating a Balkan lunch at Čevabdžinica Sarajevo ‘84 restaurant, I biked back to the hostel before noon.

On the computer, I tried to plan my route in Croatia, which will be my next country. I want to do some island hopping, but the accommodations are so expensive since it’s the high season. There aren’t many Warmshowers hosts either. I really don’t want to cycle in the mountains inland and I want to avoid the EuroVelo 8 coastal route due to the traffic. I guess I’ll have to see what happens. It’s an adventure for sure.

I don’t know what I’ll do for the rest of the afternoon. I will have to wake up early again tomorrow to catch the 6:45 AM train to Koper. I will then cycle about 15 miles to Piran and stay at a hostel for the night.

title: Day 21: Stogovci to Maribor
content:
This morning, I woke up at 4:45 so I can get on the road by 5:15. I didn’t eat anything and I wasn’t hungry. I just wanted to get to Maribor at 8 AM.

I encountered two major hills. The first one was just a couple of miles from the start. The sign indicated a 20% grade so naturally I got off my bike and pushed.

I wondered if I ever bicycle in Central and South Americas how many more steep hills will I encounter. Even though my bike’s Shimano Alfine 11 gear box only has a range of 409%, compared to a Pinion gear box that has a 600% gear range, I would still be pushing my bike because I’m not physically fit to ride up the steep hills. I might not bike tour in Latin America after all if I don’t like doing hills.

The second big hill wasn’t as steep, but it had a similar elevation. I was able to ride up the entire hill, which surprised myself.

The scariest part about a hill is actually going down. I’m glad my bike has disc brakes and they provided more stopping power than caliper rim brakes. Still, I had to be extra careful not to slide or crash, especially when turning.

I reached my host Tatjana’s place at 8 AM. After storing my bike in a small room and my panniers in the basement, I took a shower then did laundry.

Over breakfast, Tatjana and I chatted a lot about her life, the Lent Festival that’s coming up this weekend, and some of the guests that she hosted over the years.

Tatjana also recommended me to buy the Izletka train pass so that I can use it on public holidays and the weekend. Since tomorrow is Slovenia’s Statehood Day, I can use the pass to get to Ljubljana, which is Slovenia’s capital, then I can stay there for two nights to explore the city. Then on Saturday, I can take the train again to Koper, that’ll bring me to the border with Croatia.

I thought about that idea and it made sense because I can save some time in the Schengen Area so I can leave Europe via Athens with enough time. I also decided to buy my flight ticket from Athens to Philadelphia on August 26 at 1 PM for $414.31, the cheapest ticket I could find. Since I plan to go through non-Schengen countries, such as Montenegro and Albania, I will stay in these countries longer until it’s time to go to Greece. I figured that if I’m still crunched on time then I’ll take a train to Athens. So the plan is set. I will not be cycling to Beijing, China, after all. Athens will be my final destination on this bike tour.

In the afternoon, Tatjana and I walked to the main areas in Maribor. We saw the world’s oldest grapevine in the area of Lent. It has survived for over 400 years and still produces grapes! Then we walked to the main square and went into the town’s cathedral before having some gelato by the Maribor Castle. From there, I walked to the train station and bought the Izletka pass for €15, along with a day pass for my bicycle for €1.50. After stopping by the SPAR supermarket to get a couple of things, I came back to Tatjana’s condo.

Not sure what I’ll do for the rest of the day. Tomorrow, I’ll take the 11:35 AM train to Ljubljana and stay for two nights to explore the city. I’ll take another train to Koper on Saturday before resuming my bicycle tour.

title: Day 20: Fehring to Stogovci, Slovenia
content:
Yesterday afternoon, right after I took a shower it started to thunderstorm. Luckily, I was indoors. This is another benefit of arriving at my destination early since it tends to rain in the afternoons during this heat dome.

When the rain was over, I walked to the SPAR supermarket in town and bought some things for dinner. I ate most of them as soon as I got back. I was so full and it wasn’t even dinner time yet by most people’s schedule.

I ended up setting my tent inside the large building because there were so many flying bugs. Not sure if they were mosquitoes, but I didn’t want to take my chances. I slept around 5 PM and I never did see Christian again.

This morning, I woke up at 4:15 AM. After packing everything I left the Cambium commune an hour later.

Other than pushing my bike up a hill during the earlier part of my ride, I had no trouble riding 27 miles to the small village of Stogovci in Slovenia. Apparently, there are multiple Stogovcis in Slovenia. This one is on the northeast border.

I didn’t see any cafes or restaurants open in the early morning, but I wasn’t hungry anyway. I guess that’s the downside of riding a bicycle so early in the day. No businesses open.

The place I’m staying at is called Tree House - Ethno Holistic Village Apače. It’s not a tree house and it’s not a holistic village. I don’t know why they called it that. It’s a guesthouse.

I was lucky that there’s self check-in instructions so that when I arrived at 8 AM my room was ready. I booked a bed in a dorm. Since no one else is there I might have the room to myself.

The weather is so hot that I decided not to ride the 1.5 miles to the nearest restaurant in another village. I cooked a bag of ramen and ate some beef sticks and nut mixes for lunch. I don’t think I’ll do much of anything now that I’ve taken my shower and napped for three hours. I might just go to bed in a few hours and wake up early again for the 21 mile ride to Maribor, where I’ll be staying with a host from Couchers.
